report:
## Conclusion

**The claim is supported by the best available direct evidence.** The landmark randomized controlled trial by Tuuli et al. (NEJM, 2016) — which is the only large RCT specifically comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol for cesarean delivery — found a statistically significant reduction in surgical-site infection (SSI): **4.0% in the chlorhexidine–alcohol group vs. 7.3% in the iodine–alcohol group** (RR 0.55, P=0.02). This trial enrolled 1,147 women and is the most directly applicable study to the claim.

However, the broader evidence is more nuanced:

- The **CAPICA trial** (AJOG, 2017) compared chlorhexidine–alcohol against *aqueous* povidone–iodine (not iodine–alcohol) and found **no significant difference** (6.3% vs. 7.0%). This is less directly relevant since the comparator was not alcohol-based iodine.
- A **2024 network meta-analysis** found no significant difference between chlorhexidine–alcohol and iodine–alcohol across abdominal surgeries broadly (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.94–1.54), though this pooled non-cesarean procedures as well.
- A **2025 updated meta-analysis** (Frontiers) concluded chlorhexidine was associated with lower overall SSI risk compared to povidone–iodine.

**Bottom line:** The claim is **supported** by the highest-quality trial directly addressing this exact comparison (chlorhexidine–alcohol vs. iodine–alcohol in cesarean delivery). The benefit was most pronounced for scheduled cesareans (2.5% vs. 6.5%). Some other trials using aqueous iodine comparators did not reach significance, highlighting that the specific formulation (alcohol-based) matters.

### Sources
1. Tuuli et al., NEJM 2016: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048
2. CAPICA trial, AJOG 2017: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/
3. 2024 network meta-analysis: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282
4. 2025 updated meta-analysis, Frontiers: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1641815/full
